title: Part 2, Chapter 54
paragraphs: Which deals with matters concerning this history and nothing else

The duke and duchess decided that the challenge Don Quixote had issued against their vassal, for the reason already described, should go forward; and since the young man in question was in Flanders, where he had fled to avoid having Doña Rodriguez as a mother-in-law, they arranged to put a Gascon lackey named Tosilos in his place, first coaching him thoroughly in everything he would have to do. Two days later the duke informed Don Quixote that in four days' time his opponent would appear on the field armed as a knight, ready to maintain that the damsel was lying by half a beard—no, by a whole beard—if she claimed he had ever promised to marry her. Don Quixote was delighted by the news; he promised himself he would work wonders in the lists, and counted it a rare stroke of luck that an opportunity had arisen to show his noble hosts just what the strength of his mighty arm could accomplish. So, in high spirits and great contentment, he waited out the four days, which, measured against his impatience, seemed to stretch into four hundred centuries. Let us leave them to pass, as we leave other things, and go keep Sancho company, who, mounted on Dapple, half cheerful and half melancholy, was making his way along the road to rejoin his master, whose company pleased him more than being governor of all the islands in the world. Now it happened that before he had traveled very far from the island of his governorship (whether what he had governed was an island, city, town, or village, he never bothered to find out), he saw coming toward him along his road six pilgrims with staves—foreigners of the kind who beg for alms by singing. As they drew near they formed themselves into a row, and raising their voices all at once they began to sing in their own language something Sancho could not make out, except for a single word that came through clearly: “alms,” from which he gathered that alms were what their song was asking for. Being, as Cide Hamete tells us, exceedingly charitable, he took from his alforjas the half loaf and half cheese he had been supplied with and handed them over, signaling to them that he had nothing else to give. They accepted these very gladly, but cried out, “Geld! Geld!”
“I don't understand what you want from me, good people,” said Sancho.

At that, one of them pulled a purse from inside his shirt and showed it to Sancho, who now understood they were asking for money. Pressing his thumb against his throat and sweeping his open hand upward, he conveyed to them that he didn't have a coin to his name, and spurring Dapple forward, he pushed through them. But as he was passing, one of them, who had been studying him very intently, rushed at him, threw his arms around him, and exclaimed in a loud voice and excellent Spanish, “God bless me! What is this I'm seeing? Can it really be that I'm holding in my arms my dear friend, my good neighbor Sancho Panza? There's no doubt about it—I'm not dreaming, and I'm not drunk at the moment either.”

Sancho was astonished to hear himself called by name and to find himself embraced by a foreign pilgrim, and though he stared at him steadily without saying a word, he still could not place him. Seeing his confusion, the pilgrim cried, “What! Is it possible, Sancho Panza, that you don't recognize your neighbor Ricote, the Morisco shopkeeper from your own village?”

Sancho then looked at him more closely, began to trace the familiar features, and at last knew him perfectly; and without dismounting from his donkey he threw his arms around the man's neck and said, “Who the devil could have recognized you, Ricote, in this carnival outfit you're wearing? Tell me—who turned you into a Frenchman, and how do you dare come back to Spain? If they catch you and recognize you, things will go badly enough for you.”

“If you don't give me away, Sancho,” said the pilgrim, “I'm safe, because no one will recognize me in this dress. But let's get off the road and into that grove over there, where my companions are going to eat and rest. You'll eat with them—they're very good fellows—and I'll have plenty of time then to tell you everything that's happened to me since I left our village, obeying his Majesty's edict that threatened such harsh penalties against the unfortunate people of my nation, as you've heard.”

Sancho agreed, and after Ricote had spoken with the other pilgrims, they withdrew to the grove they had spotted, turning a good distance off the road. They threw down their staves, stripped off their pilgrim cloaks, and stood in their undergarments; all of them were handsome young men except Ricote, who was getting on in years. Every one of them carried alforjas, and all of them apparently well stocked—at least with things that provoke thirst, the kind that could summon it from two leagues away. They stretched out on the ground, and using the grass as a tablecloth they laid out bread, salt, knives, walnuts, scraps of cheese, and ham bones picked clean—too far gone for gnawing but not for sucking. They also set out a black delicacy called, so they say, caviar, made from fish eggs, a mighty waker of thirst. There was no shortage of olives either—dried ones, admittedly, with no seasoning at all, but tasty and pleasant for all that. What made the finest showing on that field of feasting, though, was half a dozen botas of wine, for each man produced his own from his alforjas; even the good Ricote, who had transformed himself from a Morisco into a German or a Dutchman, brought out his, which in size could have rivaled the other five. Then they began to eat with tremendous relish and at a very leisurely pace, savoring each mouthful—taking only tiny bits of everything on the point of the knife—and then, all at the same instant, they raised their arms and their botas into the air, the mouths of the wineskins pressed to their own mouths and every eye fixed on heaven as if they were taking aim at it. They held that posture a good long while, swaying their heads from side to side as if in tribute to the pleasure they were enjoying, while they emptied the entrails of the bottles into their own stomachs.

Sancho watched it all, “and none of it grieved him”; on the contrary, following the proverb he knew so well—when in Rome, do as you see done—he asked Ricote for his bota and took aim like the rest of them, and with no less pleasure. Four times the botas allowed themselves to be hoisted, but the fifth attempt was useless, for by then they were drier and more juiceless than a reed, which made the merriment that had carried them this far start to wilt.

Every so often one of them would clasp Sancho's right hand in his own and say, “Español y Tudesqui tuto uno: bon compaño,” and Sancho would answer, “Bon compaño, jur a Di!” and then break into a fit of laughter that lasted an hour, without sparing a single thought just then for anything that had happened to him in his governorship—for worries hold very little power over us while we are eating and drinking. At last, the wine having run out on them, drowsiness began to settle over them all, and they fell asleep right there on their table and tablecloth. Only Ricote and Sancho stayed awake, since they had eaten more and drunk less; and Ricote, drawing Sancho aside, sat down with him at the foot of a beech tree, leaving the pilgrims buried in sweet sleep. Then, without once slipping into his Morisco tongue, Ricote spoke as follows in pure Castilian:

“You know well, Sancho Panza, my neighbor and friend, how the proclamation or edict his Majesty ordered issued against the people of my nation filled us all with terror and dismay. It certainly did me, so much so that I think the full weight of the penalty had already crushed me and my children before the time allowed us for leaving Spain had even run out. So I decided—wisely, I think, like a man who knows that on a certain date the house he lives in will be taken from him and who looks ahead of time for another to move into—I decided, I say, to leave town by myself, alone and without my family, and go find some place I could move them to comfortably, not in the frantic rush with which the others departed. For I saw very clearly, as did all the older men among us, that those proclamations were not empty threats, as some claimed, but binding laws that would be enforced at the appointed time. And what convinced me of this was what I knew about the vile and reckless schemes our people were nursing—schemes of such a kind that I think it was divine inspiration that moved his Majesty to carry out so bold a resolution. Not that we were all guilty; some among us were true and steadfast Christians. But they were so few that they could not stand against those who were not, and it was not wise to nurse a viper in the bosom by keeping enemies inside the house. In short, it was with just cause that we were punished with banishment—a mild and gentle sentence in some people's eyes, but to us the most terrible that could be inflicted on us. Wherever we are, we weep for Spain; for after all, we were born there, and it is our natural homeland. Nowhere do we find the welcome our miserable condition requires, and in Barbary and everywhere else in Africa, where we expected to be received, helped, and made welcome, that is exactly where they insult us and mistreat us the worst. We never knew our good fortune until we lost it; and the longing nearly all of us feel to return to Spain is so strong that most of those who, like me, know the language—and there are many who do—come back to it, abandoning their wives and children over there, so great is their love for the country. And now I know from experience what they mean by the saying: sweet is the love of one's own land.

“I left our village, as I said, and went to France, and although they received us kindly there, I wanted to see all I could. I crossed into Italy and made my way to Germany, and there it seemed to me we could live with greater freedom, since the people there don't fuss over fine points; everyone lives as he pleases, because in most regions they enjoy liberty of conscience. I took a house in a town near Augsburg, and then I joined up with these pilgrims, who make a habit of coming to Spain in great numbers every year to visit the shrines, which they regard as their Indies—a sure and reliable source of profit. They travel through nearly the whole country, and there isn't a town they don't leave, as the saying goes, stuffed with food and drink and richer by at least a real in cash; and by the end of their travels they come away with more than a hundred crowns saved up, which they convert into gold and smuggle out of the kingdom, either hidden in the hollows of their staves or sewn into the patches of their pilgrim cloaks or by some trick of their own, and carry home to their own country despite the guards at the posts and crossings where they're searched. Now my plan, Sancho, is to retrieve the treasure I left buried—since it lies outside the town, I can do it without risk—and then to write to my daughter and wife, or cross over from Valencia to them, for I know they are in Algiers, and find some way of getting them to a French port and from there to Germany, where we will wait to see what God chooses to do with us. For after all, Sancho, I know for certain that my daughter Ricota and my wife Francisca Ricota are Catholic Christians, and though I am not quite so much of one myself, I am still more Christian than Moor, and I pray to God constantly to open the eyes of my understanding and show me how I am to serve him. But what astonishes me, what I cannot understand, is why my wife and daughter went to Barbary rather than to France, where they could have lived as Christians.”

To this Sancho replied, “Bear in mind, Ricote, that the choice may not have been theirs, because Juan Tiopieyo, your wife's brother, was the one who took them, and being a true Moor he went where the going was easiest for him. And I can tell you something else: I believe you're wasting your trip looking for what you left buried, because we heard that they confiscated a great quantity of pearls and gold coin from your brother-in-law and your wife, which they were trying to get past inspection.”

“That may well be,” said Ricote, “but I know they never touched my hoard, because I never told them where it was, for fear of accidents. So if you'll come with me, Sancho, and help me dig it up and hide it, I'll give you two hundred crowns to ease your needs—and as you know, I know they are many.”

“I would do it,” said Sancho, “but I'm not a greedy man at all. Just this morning I walked away from an office where, if greed had ruled me, I could have made the walls of my house out of gold and been eating off silver plates inside six months. So for that reason, and because I feel I'd be committing treason against my king by helping his enemies, I wouldn't go with you even if instead of promising me two hundred crowns you put four hundred in my hand right now.”
“And what office is this you've given up, Sancho?” asked Ricote.
“I've given up being governor of an island,” said Sancho, “and such an island, I swear, that you won't easily find its equal.”
“And where might this island of yours be?” asked Ricote.
“Where?” said Sancho. “Just two leagues down the road, and it goes by the name of the island of Barataria.”
“Don't talk nonsense, Sancho,” said Ricote. “Islands are out in the sea; there are no islands on the mainland.”

“What do you mean, no islands?” said Sancho. “I'm telling you, friend Ricote, I left it just this morning, and yesterday I was governing there exactly as I pleased, like a sagittarius. But even so I gave it up, because a governor's job struck me as a dangerous line of work.”
“And what did you gain from governing?” asked Ricote.

“What I gained,” said Sancho, “is the knowledge that I'm no good at governing anything, unless maybe a herd of cattle, and that whatever riches come from these governorships are bought at the price of your rest and your sleep—yes, and even your food, because on islands the governors have to eat next to nothing, especially if they have doctors watching over their health.”

“I can't follow you, Sancho,” said Ricote. “It all sounds to me like rubbish you're talking. Who would hand you islands to govern? Is the world running short of men cleverer than you to make governors of? Hold your tongue, Sancho, come back to your senses, and consider whether you'll come with me, as I asked, to help me carry off the treasure I left buried—and treasure really is the word for it, there's so much of it—and I'll give you enough to live on, as I told you.”

“And I've already told you, Ricote, that I won't,” said Sancho. “Be satisfied that I won't betray you, and go your way in God's name and let me go mine. For I know this much: what's honestly earned can be lost, but what's dishonestly gotten is lost along with its owner.”
“I won't press you, Sancho,” said Ricote. “But tell me—were you in our village when my wife and my daughter and my brother-in-law left it?”

“I was indeed,” said Sancho, “and I can tell you that your daughter left looking so beautiful that the whole village turned out to watch her go, and everyone said she was the loveliest creature on earth. She wept as she went, embracing all her friends and acquaintances and everyone who came out to see her, and she begged them all to commend her to God and Our Lady his mother—and she did it so movingly that it brought tears even to my eyes, and I'm not usually one for crying. And believe me, plenty of people would have liked to hide her away, or ride out and carry her off on the road; but fear of going against the king's command held them back. The one who seemed most stricken was Don Pedro Gregorio, that rich young heir you know of, who they say was deeply in love with her; and since she left, he hasn't been seen in our village again, and we all suspect he's gone after her to steal her away—but so far nothing has been heard of it.”

“I always suspected that gentleman had a passion for my daughter,” said Ricote, “but since I trusted my Ricota's virtue completely, knowing he loved her never troubled me. You must have heard it said, Sancho, that Morisco women seldom or never get entangled in love affairs with old Christians; and my daughter, who I believe cared more about being a Christian than about romance, wouldn't have given any thought to the attentions of this heir.”
“God grant it,” said Sancho, “because it would be a sorry business for both of them. But now let me be on my way, friend Ricote, for I want to reach my master Don Quixote tonight.”

“God go with you, brother Sancho,” said Ricote. “My companions are beginning to stir, and it's time for us to be moving on as well.” Then the two of them embraced, Sancho mounted Dapple, Ricote leaned on his staff, and so they parted.
